key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Hogan
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court reversed and remanded for a merits hearing, holding the family court had jurisdiction to order reunification and a merits hearing where no affirmative finding of abuse or neglect had ever been made, and condemning the practice of holding such findings in abeyance while children remain in foster care.
key_cases.relevance: No child may be retained in foster care in South Carolina without an affirmative determination of abuse or neglect.
key_cases.quote: We find this practice is in clear contravention of the removal statutes and could violate the fundamental right parents have to raise their children.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Gamble
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court reversed dismissal of a removal case, holding the statute requires that the merits hearing be scheduled to be held — not necessarily completed — within thirty-five days of the removal petition, and rejecting the parent's constitutional challenge.
key_cases.relevance: Gamble prevents a child from being returned home by operation of a deadline where probable cause of abuse has already been found.
key_cases.quote: The statute requires the family court to schedule a hearing on the merits to be held within thirty-five days of the removal petition.

key_cases.case_name: S.C. Dep't of Soc. Servs. v. Smith
key_cases.holding: The court held that foster parents are interested parties with statutory standing to petition for TPR, found clear and convincing evidence that an incarcerated father willfully failed to visit and that his post-petition contacts were judicially motivated, and held termination was in the child's best interest.
key_cases.relevance: Smith confirms that foster parents in South Carolina hold party-in-interest status under S.C. Code § 63-7-20(17), which changes the litigation posture of a foster placement.
key_cases.quote: Even if Foster Parents did not have standing to bring their private adoption action, it was well within Foster Parents' statutory right to file their TPR action.

key_cases.case_name: White Ex Rel. White v. Chambliss
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held South Carolina DSS officials were entitled to qualified immunity on claims arising from the removal of children and the foster placement in which one child died, because no clearly established federal right — including any right created by the South Carolina Child Protection Act — was violated.
key_cases.relevance: White holds that harm suffered by a child in a foster home was not, at the time, clearly established as state-inflicted harm, limiting federal exposure for placement decisions.
key_cases.quote: The facts presented by White reveal that the DSS defendants violated no "clearly established" law in removing White's children from her custody.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Sarah W.
key_cases.holding: The court upheld the 15-of-22-months ground as facially constitutional and reinstated termination, holding that the ground requires both a best-interests finding and that the delay in reunification be attributable to the parent rather than to the State.
key_cases.relevance: Sarah W. is the key defense for a parent whose child has lingered in foster care because of agency or docket delay rather than parental failure.
key_cases.quote: section 63-7-2570(8) may not be used to sever parental rights based solely on the fact that the child has spent fifteen of the past twenty-two months in foster care

key_cases.case_name: Department of Social Services v. Pritchett
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination and the foster parents' adoption, holding that an attempt to remedy the conditions causing removal is not enough because the statute requires that they in fact be remedied, and that a foster parent is an interested party with standing to petition for termination of parental rights.
key_cases.relevance: Pritchett is the original South Carolina holding that a foster parent is an 'interested party' who may petition for termination, the foundation for the standing rule Smith later applies, and it changes the litigation posture of every foster placement.
key_cases.quote: We therefore conclude a foster parent has standing as an interested party under § 20-7-1564 to petition for termination of parental rights.
